title: How Casinos Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and mechanics of casinos. They trace gambling from ancient knucklebones and dice, through Venice's Ridotto (the first government-sanctioned public gambling house) and the origin of the word "casino," to French-named games, the Nevada legalization era tied to Hoover (Boulder) Dam, and the mob's role in Las Vegas. They explain the house edge on blackjack, baccarat, roulette, craps, keno, slots and video poker, the rake in poker, casino comps and the slot club, casino design without clocks or windows, layered security, etiquette tips for players, Native American casinos and riverboat gambling, and the negative economic effects of casinos on local communities. The episode closes with a listener mail question about sweating ranch dressing versus smelling like Chinese food.

segments.title: Opening banter and casino stocks
segments.summary: Hosts chat about their favorite casino movies, Nevada and Atlantic City casino revenue trends, and their own gambling habits, such as blackjack, sports book bets, and roulette.

segments.title: Ancient gambling and the Venice Ridotto
segments.summary: Gambling dates to ancient times with knucklebone dice and early dice. Casinos as gambling halls emerged in Italy, where aristocrats gambled at private clubs. Venice's government-run Ridotto, a four-story gambling house open to the public, was the first casino; it was shut down after public opinion turned and the word casino came to mean a small club.

segments.title: French games and early American gambling
segments.summary: Many casino games have French names, such as roulette (little wheel), baccarat, and blackjack (twenty-one). Gambling riverboats operated on the Mississippi in the 1800s. An anti-gambling wave in the early twentieth century nearly wiped out gambling until Nevada legalized it around Boulder (Hoover) Dam construction.

segments.title: Las Vegas, the mob, and the Strip
segments.summary: Hoover Dam tourists boosted Nevada gambling. Gangsters such as Bugsy Siegel and Meyer Lansky expanded casinos, including the Flamingo. Early Strip developers cooperated to make the Strip a destination. The mob's role later ended as real estate developers with more money bought them out. Vegas was seen as sin city, but since the nineties it has become more family-oriented.

segments.title: Gambling destinations worldwide
segments.summary: Other gambling destinations include Monte Carlo in Monaco, Macau off Hong Kong, riverboat and Indian reservation casinos, and Japanese pachinko parlors.

segments.title: US gambling statistics and state laws
segments.summary: In 2009, 70 percent of US adults placed a wager, with about $900 billion wagered and $80.5 billion in gross gaming revenue, with casinos (tribal and standard) making up most of it. Forty-one states have or allow casinos; Utah and Hawaii allow some form of wagering while Hawaii does not allow it.

segments.title: House edge and how casinos make money
segments.summary: Every casino game has a built-in statistical edge for the house. Baccarat has about a 1.06 percent edge, while slot machines are the biggest moneymaker, bringing roughly 70 percent of revenue. State laws require slots to pay out a set percentage over time. Blackjack has about a 2 percent house edge with basic strategy; card counting is legal but casinos can ban counters.

segments.title: Casino games: slots, roulette, craps, keno, baccarat, poker
segments.summary: Slots have many themes; a Happy Days slot machine lawsuit by cast members is mentioned. Roulette has 38 spaces including 0 and 00, with house edges of 5 to 7 percent depending on bets. Craps is social, and the hosts advise sticking to a few simple bets. A keno scandal involved a Nevada Gaming Commission employee who used the random number generator pattern. Baccarat is a big-money game with a rake-like commission; poker charges a rake; video poker is close to slots.

segments.title: Casino atmosphere, comps, and security
segments.summary: Casinos use liquor, free food, and comps to keep players gambling, and they avoid clocks and windows to create a timeless atmosphere. Slot clubs track play and can rate players for comps. Security works in layers: dealers, pit bosses and table managers, then surveillance rooms with cameras, with slot areas self-managed. The movie Ocean's Eleven is cited for a camera trick.

segments.title: Casino etiquette, Native American casinos and riverboats, economic impact
segments.summary: Etiquette tips include keeping one hand visible, not touching equipment, not tickling dealers, leaving cash on the table rather than handing it to dealers, and that bets are final. Native American casinos began with Arthur James Wellness of the Cabazon tribe using a civil law loophole. Riverboat gambling involves limited cruise time and loss limits. Studies find casinos can hurt local economies, with most profits from addicted gamblers.

segments.title: Listener mail: sweating ranch or smelling like Chinese food
segments.summary: A listener asks whether you would rather sweat ranch dressing or always smell like Chinese food; the hosts discuss their answers.
